ai.definition: Long-Acting HIV Prevention refers to an injectable form of antiretroviral drugs that can provide protection against HIV for several weeks or months, thereby reducing the need for daily oral administration.
ai.howItWorks: The injectables contain long-acting formulations of antiretrovirals which are slowly released over time. This sustained release allows for a single injection to deliver therapeutic levels of medication over an extended period, typically every few weeks or months depending on the specific formulation and regimen used.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the adherence issue associated with daily oral PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis), which is critical for maintaining efficacy but can be challenging for some individuals to adhere to consistently.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing a stable, long-acting formulation of antiretrovirals that can be administered via injection. This includes optimizing drug release mechanisms and ensuring the injectable formulation remains effective over extended periods without degradation.
ai.buildProcess: Development typically involves preclinical testing to assess safety and efficacy, followed by clinical trials to validate these findings in human subjects. The process also requires regulatory approval before widespread use can be implemented.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include research and development expenses, manufacturing costs, and the need for specialized equipment or facilities for production. Clinical trial costs are significant due to the extensive testing required for safety and efficacy.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently in early commercial stages with some products already on the market or nearing approval. There is ongoing research to improve formulations, expand indications, and reduce costs.
ai.regulation: Regulatory oversight is stringent due to the critical nature of HIV prevention. Approval processes involve multiple phases including preclinical testing, clinical trials, and regulatory review by agencies such as the FDA in the United States or EMA in Europe.
ai.risks: Risks include potential side effects from long-term use, variability in drug release rates, and challenges in distribution and administration, particularly in resource-limited settings.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable but can be high for companies that successfully bring these products to market, given the significant unmet need in HIV prevention. However, cost-effectiveness may vary based on local healthcare systems and reimbursement policies.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development aims at improving efficacy, reducing injection frequency, enhancing drug stability, and expanding to other indications beyond pre-exposure prophylaxis.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking processes required for certain formulations.

glossary.def: A formulation of a drug that provides therapeutic levels over an extended period, often administered via injection.
The use of antiretroviral drugs to prevent HIV infection in people who do not have the virus but are at substantial risk of contracting it.
The extent to which a person follows prescribed directions for taking medication, such as timing and frequency.

subsystems.name: Active drug
subsystems.role: an antiretroviral modified so a single dose protects for weeks or months.

subsystems.name: Extended-release formulation
subsystems.role: the depot that dissolves so slowly the drug stays above protective levels between injections.
parts: drug nanocrystals a few hundred nanometres across

subsystems.name: Injection device
subsystems.role: delivers a large-volume intramuscular dose into the buttock.

subsystems.name: Testing and monitoring loop
subsystems.role: stops the drug being given to someone already infected, which would breed resistance.
parts: HIV rapid test and confirmatory test

subsystems.name: Supply chain
subsystems.role: keeps a refrigerated, injectable product available in the clinics that need it.

buildSteps.title: Design the molecule
buildSteps.detail: Chemists pick or engineer a compound that is potent at tiny blood concentrations and is cleared from the body very slowly.

buildSteps.title: Make the active ingredient
buildSteps.detail: The drug is synthesised by multi-step organic chemistry at pharmaceutical grade and purity.

buildSteps.title: Mill it into nanocrystals
buildSteps.detail: The crystalline drug is wet-milled with beads until particles are a few hundred nanometres wide, so they dissolve slowly after injection.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the suspension
buildSteps.detail: Surfactants, buffers and tonicity agents are added so the particles stay suspended, are injectable and are stable for years.

buildSteps.title: Sterilise and fill
buildSteps.detail: Because the product is a suspension that cannot be heat-sterilised, it is made and filled aseptically under sterile conditions.

buildSteps.title: Test in trials
buildSteps.detail: Phase 3 trials compare it with daily oral PrEP, and blood sampling defines how long protection lasts after the last dose.

buildSteps.title: Approve and prequalify
buildSteps.detail: Regulators review the data; WHO prequalification and donor funding decide whether low- and middle-income countries can buy it.

buildSteps.title: Distribute and deliver
buildSteps.detail: The product moves through a refrigerated chain to clinics, where staff are trained to give deep intramuscular injections and test for HIV first.

buildSteps.title: Monitor
buildSteps.detail: Programmes track infections that appear despite use, test for resistance, and counsel people about the long 'tail' of waning drug levels if they stop.

prerequisites.why: without a molecule that stays active for weeks, no dosing interval longer than a day is possible.
particle size and crystal form decide how fast the drug dissolves out of the muscle.

prerequisites.tech: HIV testing and viral load capacity
prerequisites.why: each injection must be preceded by testing; many clinics in high-burden regions lack reliable access.
the product is refrigerated and must be given by a trained health worker.
price and voluntary licensing determine whether the technology reaches the people who need it most.
partial protection with detectable virus is the main route to drug-resistant HIV.

pathway.milestone: cabotegravir given every two months, approved for prevention in the United States in 2021 and recommended by WHO
pathway.unlocks: an option for people who cannot take a daily pill.

pathway.milestone: twice-yearly lenacapavir, shown in the PURPOSE trials to give near-total protection
pathway.unlocks: two clinic visits a year instead of 365 pills.

pathway.milestone: generic manufacture, WHO prequalification and donor-funded roll-out
pathway.unlocks: real coverage in sub-Saharan Africa and other high-incidence regions.

pathway.milestone: year-long implants or broadly neutralising antibodies, and combinations with other prevention methods
pathway.unlocks: prevention that fits into an annual health visit rather than a daily routine.
